t:
(a) Procedures of Boards.—Paragraph (3) of section 1552(a) of title 10, United States Code, is amended—
        (1) by inserting “(A)” after “(3)”; and 
        (2) by adding at the end the following new subparagraphs:“(B) If a board makes a preliminary determination that a claim under this section lacks sufficient information or documents to support the claim, the board shall notify the claimant, in writing, indicating the specific information or documents necessary to make the claim complete and reviewable by the board.“(C) If a claimant is unable to provide military personnel or medical records applicable to a claim under this section, the board shall make reasonable efforts to obtain the records. A claimant shall provide the board with documentary evidence of the efforts of the claimant to obtain such records. The board shall inform the claimant of the results of the board’s efforts, and shall provide the claimant copies of any records so obtained upon request of the claimant.“(D) Any request for reconsideration of a determination of a board under this section, no matter when filed, shall be reconsidered by a board under this section if supported by materials not previously presented to or considered by the board in making such determination.”.  
    (b) Publication of Final Decisions of Boards.—Such section is further amended by adding at the end the following new paragraph:“(5) Each final decision of a board under this subsection shall be made available to the public in electronic form on a centralized Internet website. In any decision so made available to the public there shall be redacted all personally identifiable information.”. 
    (c) Training of Members of Boards.—
        (1) In general.—Not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act, each Secretary concerned shall develop and implement a comprehensive training curriculum for members of boards for the correction of military records under the jurisdiction of such Secretary in the duties of such boards under section 1552 of title 10, United States Code. The curriculum shall address all areas of administrative law applicable to the duties of such boards. 
        (2) Uniform curricula.—The Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of Homeland Security shall jointly ensure that the curricula developed and implemented pursuant to this subsection are, to the extent practicable, uniform. 
        (3) Training.—
            (A) In general.—Each member of a board for the correction of military records shall undergo retraining (consistent with the curriculum developed and implemented pursuant to this subsection) regarding the duties of boards for the correction of military records under section 1552 
of title 10, United States Code, at least once every five years during the member’s tenure on the board. 
            (B) Current members.—Each member of a board for the correction of military records as of the date of the implementation of the curriculum required by paragraph (1) (in this paragraph referred to as the “curriculum implementation date”) shall undergo training described in subparagraph (A) not later than 90 days after the curriculum implementation date. 
            (C) New members.—Each individual who becomes a member of a board for the correction of military records after the curriculum implementation date shall undergo training described in subparagraph (A) by not later than 90 days after the date on which such individual becomes a member of the board.  
        (4) Reports.—Not later than 18 months after the date of the enactment of this Act, each Secretary concerned shall submit to Congress a report setting forth the following:
            (A) A description and assessment of the progress made by such Secretary in implementing training requirements for members of boards for the correction of military records under the jurisdiction of such Secretary. 
            (B) A detailed description of the training curriculum required of such Secretary by paragraph (1). 
            (C) A description and assessment of any impediments to the implementation of training requirements for members of boards for the correction of military records under the jurisdiction of such Secretary.  
        (5) Secretary concerned defined.—In this subsection, the term “Secretary concerned” means a “Secretary concerned” as that term is used in section 1552 of title 10, United States Code.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that claimant notices, reconsideration requests, and public posting of decisions amount to outside participation. But these are procedures for adjudicating an individual's own claim to correct military records, which is closer to an application or appeal than to consultation on a federal policy decision. Posting final decisions online is one-way disclosure, the board members are federal personnel, and the reports go to Congress, which is inside the federal government.
fable.s: Any request for reconsideration of a determination of a board under this section, no matter when filed, shall be reconsidered by a board under this section if supported by materials not previously presented to or considered by the board in making such determination.

opus.w: The claimant's ability to submit records and ask for reconsideration is part of deciding that person's own claim to correct their military record. That is like an application or an appeal, not outside participation in a federal policy decision. The rest of the section covers board training, reports to Congress and publishing decisions, all of which stay inside the federal government or only disclose information. No advisory body, public comment or consultation with outside parties is created.
opus.s: Any request for reconsideration of a determination of a board under this section, no matter when filed, shall be reconsidered by a board under this section if supported by materials not previously presented to or considered by the board in making such determination.
opus.b: 1. **Tempting reading:** The section lets an outside party, the claimant, file claims, receive notices and request reconsideration from a board. That looks like an outsider formally objecting to a federal decision. It fails the DEFINITION because these are individual record-correction claims, which work like applications for relief or an appeal of the claimant's own case (as in Example 11). They do not bring outsiders into a policy decision. The board members are federal officials, the training requirements stay inside the government, and the reports go to Congress. Posting final decisions online is disclosure, not public input.

qwen_chat.w: This section outlines procedural requirements for boards correcting military records, specifically regarding how claimants submit evidence and how decisions are published. The interaction with claimants is part of an administrative application or appeal process, which the definition explicitly excludes ('It does not include applications for benefits or grants'). Publishing decisions to the public is a transparency measure after the fact, not consultation before a decision. There is no requirement to consult with outside entities, states, or the public before the board makes its determinations.
qwen_chat.s: (B) If a board makes a preliminary determination that a claim under this section lacks sufficient information or documents to support the claim, the board shall notify the claimant, in writing, indicating the specific information or documents necessary to make the claim complete and reviewable by the board.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that making final decisions available to the public (subsection b) constitutes participation because it involves the general public. However, the definition explicitly states that participation involves consulting or coordinating with outsiders *before* making a decision. Publishing a decision after it has been made is transparency, not participation in the decision-making process. Furthermore, the interactions described in subsection (a) are procedural steps for claimants (individuals seeking benefits/corrections) to provide evidence to a board. The definition explicitly excludes "applications for benefits or grants." Correcting military records is akin to an administrative appeal or application process, not a policy-making consultation. The board members themselves are likely federal officials or appointed experts acting in an official capacity, and the text does not describe an advisory body of outside experts influencing a broader federal policy decision.
